item.title: Anthony Albanese talks a big game about sovereignty. But Australia remains in thrall to its ‘unreliable boyfriend’ | Julianne Schultz
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Sovereignty has become the buzzword of political rhetoric at precisely the moment it has become harder than ever to define, let alone control, and most Australians feel unsafe in the world.

It is a word that regularly trips off the prime minister’s tongue as he jets around the world to global forums.

At these gatherings leaders of proud but worried nations try to recalibrate how to deal with the old superpower. One that has become, in a phrase Canada’s trade minister, Chrystia Freeland, used as the title of her new book, an “unreliable boyfriend”. She describes a partner who became a bully. Coercive control at a global level takes many forms.

Once sovereignty would have been defined by territory, shaped by governments, reinforced by armies, strong institutions, electoral systems and a robust culture. Those are all still important but have been undermined.

Monopolistic global platforms now provide the infrastructure of daily life, defence, commerce, public administration, education, media, culture and everything else. Cory Doctorow graphically describes this chilling capture in his book Enshitification and, although he is hopeful that this can be reversed, it will be a tough fight.

Even with the best regulatory systems imaginable, this digital infrastructure, shaped by commercial imperatives and protected and reinforced by the unreliable boyfriend’s laws and institutions, is not within national control. The prime minister likes to boast about Australia as a world leader in digital sovereignty, citing the social media ban for under-16s – an important, but very limited, first step. In practice what sounded like sovereignty feels more like accommodation.

When Microsoft went dark last week the wheels of government, commerce and ordinary life ground to a halt. At least half a billion people were directly affected – all at once and all around the world. Economies were paralysed.

At first it seemed like a bit of a joke but then the reality dawned. Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, Defender XDR control the fabric of modern life – email, calendars, meetings, access to files and documents.

Just the week before, David Thodey, the University of Sydney’s chancellor and a former head of CSIRO and Telstra, posed a question at a Royal Society forum considering the tipping points of existential risk. He wondered about the sovereign risk Australia faced by relying so absolutely on US technology platforms for defence and cloud services. “What would happen if Microsoft, Salesforce, Google and Anthropic all went down?” he asked.

A chill spread over the room.

The answer required a much bigger debate than we are accustomed to – about national priorities, money, ambition and delivery.

Anthony Albanese had raised a similar concern with unusual precision when he launched his approach to AI policy, saying: “If we are always dependent on someone, somewhere else, we will always be vulnerable.”

Although there has been a lot of noise since, it is unclear that the underlying sovereignty problem is being adequately addressed.

Accommodating the tech giants without giving too much away seems to be the focus.

There is an inclination to give up, as Greg Sheridan wrote in The Australian: “There is almost nothing Australia can do.”

The creative community is spearheading a campaign to address the fundamental cultural issue – the theft of copyright material to train AI models. The digital duty of care inquiry is highlighting the vulnerability of businesses which can be unilaterally removed from the platform they depend on. The research community is pointing to the catastrophic underfunding of Australian research and development.

This is not just an Australian problem. There are lessons from elsewhere, as the University of Melbourne research fellow Andrew Cullen noted: “By actively funding decentralised cloud infrastructure and homegrown software, European governments are ensuring that an American tech failure cannot knock out a local hospital. The world must adopt a similar blueprint.”

Instead, the Australian government is strengthening ties with its unreliable boyfriend. It is pouring buckets of money into a submarine and defence infrastructure project that will reshape the Australian military and economy for generations.

The links between defence and AI cannot be underestimated. As they entwine, sovereignty will become more elusive.

Aukus is already skewing industry policy towards creating military industrial research and enterprises. US anti-trans employment policies undermine Australian defence employment policy. Immunising defence sites from local laws and criminalising photographing military sites would revoke established freedoms.

The independent inquiry into Aukus concluded that the $368bn agreement is a deception that threatens to surrender Australian sovereignty.

The government did not but in the inquiry but a thousand others did, including eminent experts, former prime ministers, ministers, generals, admirals and ambassadors. They can’t all be wrong. The failure to engage and take part in a robust debate highlights a sovereign vulnerability.

The Australian National University’s National Security College released a survey this year that showed that Australians were worried about security and wanted more money spent at home to provide greater resilience.

The inquiry’s Surrendering Australia report showed that the billions allocated to Aukus could instead fund 44 conventional submarines, 180 major hospitals, 1.47m homes, upgrade every public school, eight years of the national disability insurance scheme, and solar power and batteries for every home.

We should at least have an open debate about whether that would strengthen resilience and sovereignty more than dependence on an unreliable boyfriend.

- Julianne Schultz is the author of The Idea of Australia

item.title: The island that Hitler couldn't defeat: why an entire country won an award for bravery in WW2
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The island that Hitler couldn't defeat: why an entire country won an award for bravery in WW2

The Mediterranean island endured constant bombardment by the Luftwaffe, who were ordered to force a surrender. For refusing to give in, however, Malta holds a unique honour

The George Cross is among the most prestigious British decorations, second to the Victoria Cross. Whereas that is awarded to members of the military for valour in the face of the enemy, the George Cross can go to civilians for “acts of the greatest heroism or the most conspicuous courage in circumstances of extreme danger”.

It was introduced by King George VI, superseding the Empire Gallantry Medal, in 1940. At the time of the Battle of Britain and the Blitz, it became increasingly apparent that the bravery of civilians needed to be recognised as well as the soldiers.

Since then, there have been more than 400 recipients of the medal, but one occasion when it went to a whole country: Malta.

Malta under siege

During the Second World War, the Mediterranean island and British colony was of vital strategic importance to the Allies, as a base from which the North African campaigns could be waged. As such, the Axis powers of Nazi Germany and Italy targeted Malta with heavy attack from their air forces as early as 1940, in preparation for an invasion.

From January to July 1942, Adolf Hitler ordered an escalation of hostilities to ensure that Malta would be “neutralised”. The Luftwaffe carried out hundreds of air raids – in fact, there was only one 24-hour period in those six months without bombing.

The island suffered catastrophic damage with thousands of buildings destroyed, while the military defences stretched to breaking point. Ammunition ran so low that just a few anti-aircraft rounds could be fired each day until the arrival of a few dozen Spitfires offered some resistance in the skies.

The population of Malta faced the constant terror of bombardment and, as food became scarce, was pushed to the brink of starvation. People spent most of their time in underground shelters, desperately carved out of the limestone rock of the island.

Yet Malta did not surrender.

“To honour her brave people”

In a letter dated 15 April 1942 to governor-general William Dobbie, the king announced the remarkable decision to recognise the island itself, writing: “To honour her brave people, I award the George Cross to the Island Fortress of Malta to bear witness to a heroism and devotion that will long be famous in history.”

Dobbie responded: “By God’s help Malta will not weaken but will endure until victory is won.”

The siege continued until May 1943, and the defence only held out thanks to a dangerous supply mission, codenamed Operation Pedestal, which brought much-needed fuel, food and medical supplies. Its success came at a great cost: nine of the 14 merchant ships failed to reach Malta, while four of the accompanying warships were sunk.

Incidentally, for his part in Operation Pedestal, Dudley William Mason – captain of the fuel tanker Ohio, which sustained heavy damage on its way to the island’s harbour – would be awarded the George Cross himself.

Legacy of the George Cross

Then with their defeat in North Africa, Hitler and Benito Mussolini were forced to abandon hopes of seizing Malta once and for all. By then, there had been a recorded 3,340 air raids, resulting in 1,581 deaths.

To this day, Malta’s unique honour is remembered in the country’s flag, with the George Cross included in the top-left corner. This is not the sole example, however, of a non-individual recipient of the decoration. Eilzabeth II awarded it to the Royal Ulster Constabulary – the police force in Northern Ireland during the Troubles – and, in 2021, to the staff of the National Health Service.

Authors

Jonny Wilkes is a former staff writer for BBC History Revealed, and he continues to write for both the magazine and HistoryExtra. He has BA in History from the University of York.

item.title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.

Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase. On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down. In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.

But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked, spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries.

Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever. And the digital border walls are crumbling – with the AI industry to blame. Frontier AI models can find and exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them, and the rush to patch raises the risk of exactly the kind of disruptions we’re now seeing.

The AI industry is built around relentlessly scaling AI models, discovering what new capabilities emerge, then deploying the models for commercial gain. So far, this process has wrecked education and sloppified the internet; now it threatens to break it altogether.

Instead of waiting to see what the companies break next, we should freeze the reckless gain-of-function experiments they call “frontier AI development”.

Already, hackers are “all using AI now”, declares Ireland’s cybersecurity chief. Google’s top threat analyst agrees: “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited.”

And benefit they have. In recent months, apparent amateurs have used AI to hack more than 100 companies, from the tractor maker Deere to South Korean banks, with the hackers spending as little as $50 per successful infiltration.

Suspected North Korean hackers carried out the biggest heist ever, stealing $6.3bn from the crypto exchange Binance, less than half of which has been frozen or recovered.

Cyber-attacks took down hospital emergency rooms in New Mexico and Germany. AI-enabled hackers broke into the European Commission, disrupting services for more than 10 days.

And on Monday, attackers exploited a flaw in third-party software to serve malware to visitors of 178 organisations’ sites, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC.

Last month, researchers using AI discovered a severe flaw in the programming language powering 70% of all websites. (The NSA outage, officials now say, was caused by a rushed patch for that very flaw.) The CEO of internet security provider Cloudflare said he knew of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software … I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

“The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues … is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors,” the CEO of a multi-billion dollar Japanese financial services company said after his company was hacked last month.

While AI has been accelerating cybercrime for years, the recent deluge can be largely attributed to highly capable, easily modified open-weight models released by Chinese developers.

But the AI industry on both sides of the Pacific is responsible for the internet’s “Black October” and whatever other cyber horrors await us.

In their quest to render us obsolete, Anthropic and OpenAI were the first to develop and release superhuman hacker AIs – knowing that Chinese developers would piggyback off their progress to release guardrail-free hacker AIs in a matter of months.

The US companies’ plan was to use AI to fix the world’s critical software in time. They didn’t. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last month. His new plan is to use AI agents to defend against AI hackers. In other words, the flamethrower industry decided to start selling firehoses too.

When a Twitter/X user told Anthropic’s deputy cyber chief: “You and your cohorts created this monster,” his reply was shockingly candid: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” Thanks for the heads up.

These hacks and disruptions may soon appear quaint. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in September, “it’s my worry that in 6–12 months [an AI agent] swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet.”

But accelerating AI capabilities aren’t actually a “given” – they’re a product of trillions of dollars in investment and deliberate effort, which is predictably producing enormous new dangers. Anthropic’s IPO filing acknowledges that the entire insurance industry may not be big enough to cover the catastrophic or existential risks the company is creating.

Those risks extend beyond the cyber realm. This summer, researchers at Stanford University synthesized the first AI-designed viruses, and Anthropic quietly set up an automated biology wet lab – a space for physical experiments – in what it says is a bid to find treatments for rare diseases. Meanwhile, AI models steadily improve at assisting in the development of bioweapons. We’ll survive superhuman hacker AIs, but maybe not the bioterrorist variety.

All of these risks will arrive faster if the industry achieves its primary goal: turning AI development over entirely to the machines, in a process known as recursive self-improvement.

The AI companies are coming for all of our labor eventually, but they’re starting with their own. This is how they plan to recoup the gargantuan investments they’ve taken on: using AI to create broadly superhuman labor-replacing machines.…

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-20 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another.

This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives.

The bar is high; in 2007, the ICJ found Serbia responsible for failing to prevent genocide in Srebrenica in 1995, but not for directly committing it. Genocidal intent must be the “only reasonable inference” from a pattern of conduct. Legal scholars have pointed out that that need not preclude its coexistence with other aims. The court has not changed the standard, but shown how it can be applied.

Yet even before the ruling, the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, had accused Navi Pillay, this year’s Nobel peace laureate, of intending to lower the legal threshold so that it could be “weaponised against American and allied soldiers”. There is grave concern that the US will impose sanctions on Ms Pillay and fellow judges, as it has on the international criminal court, which holds individuals rather than states accountable. Israel is currently before the ICJ on genocide charges, and the relevance of Thursday’s finding to Gaza is obvious.

But this case is first and foremost important as an attempt to bring some measure of justice for the Rohingya, whose suffering began decades ago and continues. Survivors in refugee camps greeted the findings with applause as they watched the session on Thursday. The UN warned in August that human rights in Myanmar had hit a new low, citing the “ever-worsening brutal abuse” of members of the minority. The military has forcibly conscripted those it despises in the civil war – fuelling atrocities against them by one of the junta’s adversaries, the Arakan army. Those who have found safety abroad also face returning to danger. India has repatriated Rohingya refugees, and there are growing concerns that Malaysia may send back many more, following a visit by Min Aung Hlaing, the leader of Myanmar’s junta.

Myanmar now has two years to set out plans for full restitution, including the safe and voluntary return home that survivors still seek. If and when it fails, the court will take up the issue. But governments must play their part. The UK’s expulsion of Myanmar’s military attache was a small but welcome step. It must do much more to step up the pressure on the junta and other parties in Myanmar to ensure the safety of the Rohingya, and urge other governments to do likewise. States that believe in international law must do all they can to back this ruling and ensure that it has real consequences, both to protect the Rohingya and to show support for the court itself.

item.title: 7 Old-Fashioned Words That Describe Beauty
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Society has always had, and will always have, shifting standards of beauty. Each year, decade, and century, across oceans and cultures, we're given new ideals to marvel at and obsess over, from facial features to style to settings.

While this seems unavoidable, especially in the digital era, true beauty remains in the eye of the beholder.

Beauty in the Eye of the Era

Whether weâre admiring a person or a scene, what we find beautiful is subjective. A person you find particularly attractive might not be equally remarked upon by an acquaintance. Similarly, a destination someone else considers stunning might not appeal to you whatsoever. And perhaps thatâs the beauty of beauty!Â

This individuality inspires different looks, trends, and tourist destinations that take turns in the spotlight. Over time, big hair gave way to long, sleek tresses; clean-shaven faces to mustaches and beards; and figures are constantly commented on and held to new beauty standards, often to a detriment. For the same reason, map dots that were once obscure are now visited by travelers from all over the world.Â

Throughout history, beauty and attention have been synonymous with power, wealth, and identity, Cleopatra being a defining example. But physical beauty says far less about a personâs character than what lies within.Â

Beautyâs Vintage Vocabulary Bank

Beauty, by definition, is âthe quality or group of qualities in a person or thing that gives pleasure to the senses or the mind.â And since we all have different minds, a physical âbeauty standardâ is a very loose concept with a very strong hold on society.

Synonyms for beauty describe the physical appearance of a person or place, sometimes in a pleasing way and sometimes with hints of allure and deception; It can be a double-edged sword, after all.Â

Many of these words have nearly disappeared from modern vocabulary or have been replaced by terms like âhot,â âpretty,â and âcool,â but they bring a certain vintage charm to the conversation.

They describe not only beauty, but also love, confidence, impressiveness, and vanity, with descriptions as ravishing as their definitions.

Here are seven old-timey words that describe beauty in different ways.Â

Ravishing

Definition: "unusually attractive, pleasing, or striking."

In a sentence: I'd heard about her ravishing countenance, but was unaware of the true measure of her wit.

Formosity

Definition: "beauty or a beautiful thing."

In a sentence: Her natural formosity made her shine like a bright light in every room she entered.

Radiant

Definition: "marked by or expressive of love, confidence, or happiness, vividly bright and shining, glowing."

In a sentence: His undeniable radiance drew people in, making him a noticeable presence at every function.

Lovesome

Definition: "winsome, lovely."

In a sentence: The actress's lovesome features gave her a timeless elegance that shone through the silver screen for centuries.

Striking

Definition: "attracting attention or notice through unusual or conspicuous qualities."

In a sentence: The scene was so striking, he compared it to a dream.

Handsome

Definition: "having a pleasing and usually impressive or dignified appearance."

In a sentence: His handsome face was not easily forgotten, nor his kindness.

Specious

Definition: "having deceptive attraction or allure, showy."

In a sentence: The stranger's specious smile made him seem very approachable, but, what was hiding beneath it?

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-22 01:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: 7 European Villages That Look Even More Magical in the Snow
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Few feelings can compete with the warmth of a summerâs day beaming down on your face, beckoning you to enjoy activities that pair with temperatures above 60 Â°F.Â

And while many of us plan entire trips around this weather, a handful of alpine destinations across Europe make us question just how important the warmth really is when the alternative is a stunning, snow-covered scene that looks handpicked from the coziest film you've ever seen.

During the final season of the year, these villages turn into winter wonderlands, complete with skiing, ice skating, and, in some places, even hot-air-balloon and sleigh rides. Sure, they're a bit chillier, but the mountain views more than make up for the cold, not to mention the cafÃ©s and cute shops.

Here are seven European villages that are fun to explore year-round, but look even more magical in the snow.

Grindelwald, Switzerland

Population: 3,942

Winter weather: 29 Â°F to 40 Â°F in December

Grindelwald is perched at an elevation of 3,392 feet in Switzerlandâs German-speaking Bern region, at the base of the Eiger (a famous mountain). The village is dotted with wooden houses, hotels, cafÃ©s, and restaurants, all set against the snow-blanketed backdrop of the Swiss Alps. Visitors can explore Bussalp, an alpine pasture, and take on the Big Pintenfritz toboggan run, one of the longest in Europe, as well as mountain-cart rides, cliff walks with unbelievable views of the Bernese Alps, and access to the UNESCO World Heritage site of Aletsch Glacier.

The Jungfrau Ski Region officially opens for the season on November 29, offering miles upon miles of runs and winter fun for skiers of all ages.

Hallstatt, Austria

Population: 741

Winter weather: 25 Â°F to 36 Â°F in December

Hallstatt is such a wonder that it's been a UNESCO World Heritage Site for almost 30 years. Though this alpine village looks like a still frame from a postcard, it's teeming with life, and thereâs no shortage of winter activities for tourists. Travelers can ski at Dachstein Krippenstein, across Lake Hallstatt, or at Dachstein West, a big family destination; both are expected to open in December. If winter sports aren't your cup of tea (or should we say, cup of hot cocoa?), you can meander through the old townâs shops and restaurants where you'll find handmade goods and warm, delicious Austrian cuisine. A Christkindlmarkt is held annually on December 8.Â

Visitors can ride the gondola up to the Skywalk for panoramic views of the lake and Hallstatt in all its snow-dusted glory.

MegÃ¨ve, France

Population: around 2,893

Winter weather: 31 Â°F to 46 Â°F in December

MegÃ¨ve, high in the French Alps, is an alpine resort village in Haute-Savoie with a rich history extending beyond skis and chalets. Developed in the 1910s and â20s as a French alternative to Switzerlandâs St. Moritz, the resort village was designed by philanthropist Baroness NoÃ©mie de Rothschild and hosted events during the 1968 Winter Olympics. The town was actually founded by Benedictine monks and dates back to the Middle Ages.

The ski area spans three mountains, including Mont dâArbois, the largest, with slopes supporting varying skill levels. The resorts can be a bit pricey, but budget-friendly hotels are available for travelers looking to save a few euros.

Non-skiers can enjoy ice skating, curling, dog sledding, snowshoeing, hot-air balloon rides, and luxury spa retreats, perfectly paired with a day of high-end shopping.Â MegÃ¨ve is easily accessible from the Gevena airport.

Malbun, Liechtenstein

Population: 44

Winter weather: 31 Â°F to 44 Â°F in December

Did you know Malbun is Liechtensteinâs only ski resort? (Considering the countryâs size, this might not be too surprising.) Located in the Alps near the Austrian border, the area features slopes stretching for over a mile. It's a family-friendly destination that typically opens in mid- to late December. Steep mountain peaks surround the valley, making the views around every corner breathtaking.

In addition to skiing, Malbun has several walking trails, including the popular Sassweg, as well as sledding and snowshoeing. Restaurants and businesses use Swiss francs, and German is the primary language, though English is understood at tourist spots.

Getting to Malbun isn't entirely a straight path: the closest airport is in Zurich. From there, travelers take a train to Sargans in Switzerland or Feldkirch in Austria, then a bus to Vaduz (Liechtensteinâs capital), followed by another 30-minute bus ride to Malbun.

Ortisei, Italy

Population: 4,710

Winter weather: 27 Â°F to 44 Â°F in December

Nestled in the Dolomites of northern Italy, the small alpine town of Ortisei sits more than 4,000 feet up in Val Gardena, South Tyrol. Surrounded by several other tiny villages, it remains a popular year-round destination. In winter, Ortisei offers access to the Dolomiti Superski area and the Sellaronda circuit, an extensive network of ski routes connecting several valleys. Visitors can also try snowboarding and tobogganing.Â

If skiing and snowboarding aren't your thing, this idyllic alpine village also offers quaint stays, bakeries, cafÃ©s, and shops. Wood carving is a tradition in Ortisei, and you'll definitely notice the elaborate wooden altars and sculptures throughout the town.

Kranjska Gora, Slovenia

Population: 5,143

Winter weather: 26 Â°F to 38 Â°F in December

Tucked away in the Julian Alps, Kranjska Gora is situated near the Italian and Austrian borders and close to Triglav National Park. It isn't as high in the mountains as some other villages on this list, so the resort relies on snowmaking during warmer periods. Its 18 slopes accommodate skiers of all ages, with the season starting in December. Winter sports enthusiasts can also visit Planica, known for its world-renowned ski jumping and ski flying. Other winter activities in or around the village include sledding, ice skating, snowshoeing, and hiking.…

item.title: America's Biggest Senior Populations, Mapped By State
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

As the nation ages, some states grapple with the issue more than others, with different states seeing a large part of their population reaching age 65 and beyond.

Roughly 19% of the United States population is over the age of 65, with almost 65 million Americans counting themselves among this older age group. But some states see a higher percentage than that when it comes to their population, affecting issues like health care, a drop in tax revenue, or an increase in services used by an aging population.

Some states may be seeing these problems now with a percentage of their senior population exceeding the national average, while other states may have younger populations. So, where does your state land? Here are some of the states with the biggest percentages of their population being on the older side, according to data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

New Englandâs Gray Wave

Two New England states top the list for the percentage of their populations over 65.

Maine came in first place with 23.5% of the population over 65, followed by second-place Vermont with 22.9% over that age. For Maine, that equates to around 330,000 residents, while Vermont has 148,000 Vermonters above that age. Nearby New Hampshire ranks seventh with 21.5% of its population over that age.

Florida is well known as a place for retirees who want to move somewhere warmer when they get older, and that's reflected in the population. The state ranks fourth by percentage, with 21.8% of its population checking in as 65 or older. That equates to 5.1 million Floridians over 65. The only state with a higher population over 65 is California, with 6.5 million senior residents. However, that's only 16.5% of its total population, ranking it 45th overall.

The top 10 states that have the highest percentage of residents over the age of 65 as a percentage of their total population include:

1. Maine

2. Vermont

3. West Virginia

4. Florida

5. Delaware

6. Hawaii

7. New Hampshire

8. Montana

9. Pennsylvania

10. New Mexico

The Youngest States Out West

While the East Coast is facing an aging population, states out west are younger with fewer residents over the of 65 years old.

Utah leads that list with 435,000 residents over the age of 65, which equals only 12.4% of its population. That may not be a surprise considering Utah is the youngest state in the U.S. The median age for a resident there is only 32 years old, while Maine, the state with the highest percentage of residents over the age of 65, has a median age of 44.8 years old. That makes it the state with the highest median age.

The District of Columbia came in second place with only 12.9% of its population over the age of 65. Because of its small population, that only equates to 91,000 residents, which is the smallest number of 65- and older residents in the U.S. by count.

Third-place Texas also has a younger population with 14.0% of its residents over the age of 65. But like California and Florida, it also has a huge population, so 14.0% equates to 4.4 million residents. That's the third-highest number of residents that can be considered seniors.

The top 10 states with the lowest percentage of residents over the age of 65 include:

1. Utah

2. District of Columbia

3. Texas

4. Alaska

5. Georgia

6. Colorado

7. California

8. Oklahoma

9. Washington

10. Nebraska

item.title: Abbott spent 12 years neglecting Texas air pollution – a new governor can start cleaning it up
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

When air quality monitors in 10 Texas counties showed soot above the new federal health limit in 2024, Gov. Greg Abbott faced a choice. He could direct the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to develop plans to cut air pollution in all 10. Or he could heed the agency’s advice: blame six counties’ pollution mostly on sources beyond Texas, and clean up just four.

Abbott chose neither. Weeks after President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the governor asked the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare the entire state in compliance with the federal standard for fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5. If the EPA agreed, Texas would skirt the need to write a plan to control the deadliest air pollutant.

As an atmospheric scientist, I was stunned. I had seen Texas and other states do too little to control air pollution for years. But I hadn’t imagined a governor would override his own regulators to avoid making a plan altogether.

Texas air pollution had declined for decades, but during Abbott’s 12 years in office, progress in reducing PM2.5 and ozone smog largely stalled.

Now, the election of Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa to succeed Abbott in January 2027 offers a chance to get Texas pollution trending downward again.

Hinojosa has a history of supporting efforts to clean up pollution, including a climate plan proposed in 2021 to cut emissions. But progress won’t come easily. Abbott’s appointees still run the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, and Republicans still control the state Senate.

A deadly legacy

PM2.5 is tiny, with diameters of 2.5 microns or less, so it can be inhaled deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure has been linked to heart attacks, strokes, respiratory problems and many other ailments.

Some PM2.5 is emitted directly as particles, such as in diesel exhaust and wildfire smoke. Other particles form in the atmosphere from sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbon gases emitted by power plants, vehicles and other sources.

Abbott’s dodge of PM2.5 standards fit a pattern of going easy on polluters.

Houston and Dallas have missed deadline after deadline to meet federal ozone standards. State regulators blame much of the smog on foreign sources. This fall, Abbott persuaded the Trump administration to reconsider how severely the two regions’ smog is classified, a step that could loosen the pollution controls required there.

Under Abbott, state regulators have also rarely cracked down on unauthorized pollution releases. Of 21,769 such events reported by refineries, chemical plants and other facilities over six years, they classified fewer than 1% as “excessive,” the designation that requires a company to fix the problem.

The fight over scrubbers

Texas’ coal power plants emit more sulfur dioxide than any other state’s. That gas forms sulfate particles, a major ingredient of PM2.5 and haze. Federal rules have required new coal plants to install scrubbers, which remove sulfur dioxide from smokestack gases, since 1979. But older plants were exempted, and several in Texas still run without them.

A 2016 Obama administration plan to reduce Texas’ haze and a narrower Biden administration proposal in 2023 would have required several plants to install or upgrade scrubbers. In 2025 the Trump administration accepted Texas’ own haze plans, which required no new scrubbers. Critics of the federal plans had warned that some plants would close instead because of the cost, reducing electricity supplies.

But scrubbers are a long-established technology, and their health benefits dwarf their costs. When I worked at Georgia’s environmental agency in the mid-2000s, we negotiated a timetable for Georgia Power to install scrubbers and retire outdated plants. Atlanta’s PM2.5 levels fell about 40% over the next decade, and the lights stayed on just fine.

Research by my group at Rice University has found that PM2.5 from Texas coal plants, formed mostly from their sulfur dioxide, kills hundreds of people a year. Wind and solar power or geothermal energy could replace their output, with batteries filling in when winds are slow and sunshine weak.

No polluter has benefited more from Abbott’s neglect than the W.A. Parish power plant, whose smokestacks loom over my hikes at Brazos Bend State Park southwest of Houston.

Three of its four coal units have no scrubbers at all. Parish emitted three times as much sulfur dioxide as all other facilities in the Houston region combined in 2024. Our modeling linked its pollution to 177 deaths a year. Since sulfate, which forms from sulfur dioxide, is the second-largest ingredient in Houston’s PM2.5, any serious cleanup plan would have to tackle Parish.

Clearing the air

Hinojosa’s first test will come within weeks of her inauguration, when the U.S. EPA faces a court-ordered deadline to announce which counties violate its PM2.5 standard.

The number of Texas counties exceeding the limit is now at 14. Wildfire smoke and other exceptional events may explain some of the problem, but most of those counties need plans to cut the local emissions driving their PM2.5 levels.

Hinojosa can withdraw Abbott’s zero-county request and ask the EPA to designate counties as failing to meet the standard where the data warrants it, triggering a need to write cleanup plans.

In my view, those plans should start with overdue controls on emissions at the dirtiest coal plants. The state also needs to cut pollution from refineries, chemical plants, industrial flares and ports to meet the standards. Expanding grants to replace old diesel engines would cut soot and smog.

Better plans would include more monitors. Many counties, including Fort Bend, Texas’ eighth-most-populous county and home to Parish, don’t have a single PM2.5 monitor. Others don’t measure what their PM2.5 is made of. Because PM2.5 is a stew of carbon, sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, dust and other compounds, knowing the mix is key to controlling it cost-effectively.…
